title: The Untold Story of Abraham
paragraphs: The Untold Story of Abraham
There are some people in Scripture whose names became so familiar that we accidentally stopped feeling their humanity.
Abraham is one of them.
We say “father of faith” so often that we forget he once stood in the middle of a dark night wondering if God had abandoned him.
We quote his obedience while ignoring the terror inside it.
We celebrate the promise while skipping over the silence.
But the untold story of Abraham is not just about a man who believed God.
It is about a broken human being who kept walking even when heaven felt painfully quiet.
And maybe that is why his story still shakes souls thousands of years later.
Because deep down, many people are still living in Ur.
Still trapped. Still afraid. Still successful externally while spiritually starving internally. Still hearing whispers from God while pretending not to.
The first mention of Abraham does not even begin with greatness.
It begins with interruption.
Genesis 12:1 says:
“Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house, unto a land that I will shew thee.”
The Hebrew phrase for “Get thee out” is:
לֶךְ־לְךָ
Transliterated:
Lech-Lecha
This phrase carries deeper meaning than most English translations reveal.
It does not merely mean “leave.”
It carries the idea:
“Go for yourself.” “Go toward your true self.” “Go into the purpose I created for you.”
God was not only calling Abraham away from a location.
He was calling him away from the false version of himself.
Away from inherited idols. Away from familiar chains. Away from generational patterns. Away from comfort. Away from predictable living.
And some people reading this know exactly what that feels like.
Because God has been disturbing your comfort lately.
You cannot enjoy the sin the same way anymore. You cannot fit into the old conversations anymore. You cannot ignore conviction anymore.
Something inside you has been hearing:
“Leave.”
Leave the bitterness. Leave the compromise. Leave the secret addiction. Leave the lukewarm Christianity. Leave the version of yourself that survives without surrender.
And the terrifying part is this:
God did not initially tell Abraham where he was going.
Hebrews 11:8 says:
“By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went.”
Not knowing.
That phrase destroys modern Christianity.
Because most people want guarantees before obedience.
But biblical faith has always moved before explanations arrived.
Abraham walked with incomplete details.
And honestly, that is where many believers lose their courage.
Because uncertainty exposes whether we truly trust God or merely trust outcomes.
Some of the deepest faith seasons are not loud miracles.
They are quiet obedience.
The untold story of Abraham is filled with waiting.
Years. Decades. Silence.
God promised him descendants while Sarah’s womb remained empty.
Imagine the emotional warfare.
Every birthday becoming another reminder. Every gray hair screaming impossibility. Every month ending in disappointment.
And yet God had said:
“So shall thy seed be.”
Genesis 15 records one of the rawest moments in Scripture.
Abraham looks into the heavens while God speaks about descendants more numerous than stars.
The Hebrew says:
וְהֶאֱמִן בַּיהוָה
Vehe’emin BaYHWH
“And he believed in the LORD.”
The Hebrew word here for “believed” comes from:
אָמַן
Aman
The same root where we get “Amen.”
It means:
To support. To uphold. To lean the full weight upon.
Abraham’s faith was not intellectual agreement.
It was collapsing his full weight onto God when everything visible contradicted the promise.
That changes everything.
Real faith is not pretending doubts do not exist.
Real faith is choosing to lean on God while doubts scream in your face.
And Abraham did struggle.
Scripture does not hide his failures.
He lied. He doubted. He tried to manufacture God’s promise through Hagar. He made fearful decisions.
The Bible never sanitizes its heroes.
Because the point was never human perfection.
The point was God’s faithfulness.
One of the most misunderstood parts of Abraham’s story is the covenant in Genesis 15.
Most people miss how shocking this moment really was.
In ancient covenant rituals, animals were split in half and both parties walked between the pieces, symbolizing:
“If I break this covenant, let this happen to me.”
But in Genesis 15, Abraham falls into deep sleep.
And only God passes through.
A smoking furnace. A burning lamp.
God alone walked the covenant path.
Why does that matter?
Because God knew Abraham would fail.
And yet He still bound Himself to the promise.
That is grace.
The covenant rested ultimately on God’s faithfulness, not Abraham’s perfection.
Somebody reading this has been drowning in shame because you think your failures disqualified you.
But Abraham’s story proves something powerful:
God already knew your weakness before He called you.
He was never shocked by your humanity.
This does not excuse sin.
But it destroys the lie that grace belongs only to flawless people.
Then came the waiting.
Long waiting.
Some theologians estimate nearly 25 years between the promise and Isaac’s birth.
Twenty-five years.
Most people cannot endure twenty-five minutes of silence anymore.
But God develops giants in hidden seasons.
The name change itself carried prophetic weight.
Abram:
אַבְרָם
“Exalted father.”
Abraham:
אַבְרָהָם
“Father of many.”
God changed his identity before changing his circumstances.
And sometimes God speaks to who you are becoming before your life visibly reflects it.
That process feels painful.
Because heaven will call you healed while you are still bleeding. Heaven will call you chosen while you still feel rejected. Heaven will call you free while chains are still falling off.
Then Isaac finally arrives.
The miracle child.
The laughter after decades of tears.
The promise fulfilled.
And then comes Genesis 22.
The chapter that leaves many people emotionally shaken.
“Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest…”
The Hebrew phrase “whom thou lovest” is:
אֲשֶׁר־אָהַבְתָּ
Asher-Ahavta
“The one you love deeply.”
This is the first explicit mention of love in the Bible.
And it appears in the context of surrender.
Not romance. Not pleasure. Not comfort.
Surrender.
That is breathtaking.
God asked Abraham to place even the promise itself on the altar.
Because gifts can never become idols.
Not even sacred gifts.
Some people idolize relationships. Others idolize ministry. Others idolize success. Others idolize dreams God Himself gave them.
But Abraham’s test revealed whether he loved God more than what God provided.
The mountain was never about child sacrifice.
God had already condemned pagan child sacrifice elsewhere in Scripture.
The deeper revelation was prophetic.
Abraham tells Isaac:
“God will provide himself a lamb.”
In Hebrew:
אֱלֹהִים יִרְאֶה־לּוֹ הַשֶּׂה
Elohim Yir’eh-Lo HaSeh
This becomes connected to:
יְהוָה יִרְאֶה
YHWH Yireh
“Jehovah Jireh”
Often translated:
“The Lord will provide.”
But the Hebrew idea is even richer.
It literally carries the sense:
“The Lord will see.” “The Lord will see ahead.” “The Lord will foresee the need before it arrives.”
God already had provision waiting on the mountain Abraham feared.
And many believers need to hear this today:
The ram was already prepared before Abraham climbed the mountain.
God’s provision is not panic response.
He already sees tomorrow.
The untold story of Abraham ultimately points beyond Abraham.
It points to Christ.
A beloved son. A father willing to surrender. A mountain. Wood carried upward. A substitute provided.
Genesis whispers the Gospel long before Calvary arrived.
Jesus Himself said in John 8:56:
“Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day: and he saw it, and was glad.”
Even Abraham’s journey was ultimately pointing toward redemption through Jesus Christ.
And maybe the reason Abraham’s story still grips hearts is because we see ourselves in it.
We know what it feels like to wait.
To fear. To fail. To wonder. To obey while trembling. To carry promises through painful seasons. To wrestle between faith and visible reality.
The untold story of Abraham is not the story of a fearless man.
It is the story of a man who kept moving toward God despite fear.
That changes everything.
Because many people secretly think faith means never struggling.
But Scripture repeatedly reveals something different.
Faithful people still cry. Faithful people still wrestle. Faithful people still ask questions. Faithful people still collapse emotionally.
Yet they keep returning to God.
And maybe that is you right now.
Maybe you are in a season where God feels silent.
Maybe the promise feels delayed. Maybe your heart is exhausted. Maybe you feel disqualified because of your failures. Maybe you have secretly wondered whether God forgot you.
Abraham’s story still answers across generations:
God is faithful even in the waiting.
Not one promise of God has ever died because human weakness existed.
And the greatest promise was never land, descendants, or earthly blessing.
The greatest promise was Jesus.
Galatians 3 reveals that ultimately the covenant pointed toward Christ through whom all nations would be blessed.
The Gospel was hidden inside Abraham’s story from the beginning.
That means your story can also become redemption territory.
Your failures are not the final sentence. Your waiting is not wasted. Your wilderness is not proof of abandonment.
God still calls broken people. Still transforms wandering hearts. Still restores ruined lives. Still writes impossible stories.
And maybe this article found you at the exact moment you needed it.
Not accidentally.
Because there are people reading this who have been smiling publicly while silently collapsing internally.
People exhausted from pretending. People tired of carrying hidden pain. People wondering whether God could still use them.
Abraham’s story says yes.
Not because humans are strong.
But because God remains faithful.
Be honest. This reached deeper than information.
Some mountains are actually places where God reveals who He has always been.
Filipino Version:
Ang Hindi Naikuwentong Bahagi ng Buhay ni Abraham
May mga tao sa Bibliya na sobrang madalas nating marinig ang pangalan kaya nakalimutan na nating tao rin pala sila.
Isa na roon si Abraham.
Madalas natin siyang tawaging “ama ng pananampalataya,” pero bihira nating isipin na may mga gabi ring halos mawalan siya ng pag-asa.
Pinupuri natin ang kanyang pagsunod, pero hindi natin nararamdaman ang takot na kasama noon.
Ikinukuwento natin ang pangako ng Diyos, pero nilalampasan natin ang mahabang katahimikan sa pagitan.
At baka iyon ang dahilan kung bakit hanggang ngayon, tinatamaan pa rin ng kuwento ni Abraham ang puso ng tao.
Dahil marami pa ring tao ang parang nasa “Ur.”
Nakakulong. Takot. Mukhang maayos sa labas pero wasak sa loob. Naririnig ang tawag ng Diyos pero nagpapanggap na hindi.
Nagsimula ang kuwento ni Abraham hindi sa tagumpay.
Nagsimula ito sa pagputol ng Diyos sa dati niyang buhay.
Genesis 12:1:
“Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country…”
Sa Hebrew:
לֶךְ־לְךָ
Lech-Lecha
Hindi lang ito simpleng “umalis ka.”
Mas malalim ang ibig sabihin.
“Humayo ka para sa tunay mong pagkatao.” “Lumakad ka patungo sa layunin ko para sa’yo.”
Hindi lang si Abraham pinapaalis ng Diyos sa isang lugar.
Pinapaalis siya ng Diyos sa lumang bersyon ng sarili niya.
Sa maling identidad. Sa nakasanayang kasalanan. Sa mga bagay na humahadlang sa tawag ng Diyos.
At baka may nagbabasa nito ngayon na nakakaramdam din niyan.
Hindi mo na ma-enjoy ang dati mong kasalanan. Hindi ka na mapalagay sa dati mong buhay. May bumabagabag sa puso mo.
At paulit-ulit mong naririnig:
“Umalis ka.”
Umalis ka sa lihim na kasalanan. Umalis ka sa pagpapanggap. Umalis ka sa pagiging malamig sa Diyos. Umalis ka sa buhay na walang surrender.
At ang pinakamahirap?
Hindi agad sinabi ng Diyos kay Abraham kung saan siya dadalhin.
Hebrews 11:8:
“…and he went out, not knowing whither he went.”
Hindi niya alam.
At doon nasusubok ang totoong pananampalataya.
Dahil karamihan gusto muna ng kasiguruhan bago sumunod.
Pero ang totoong faith sa Bibliya, sumusunod muna bago makita ang buong plano.
Lumakad si Abraham kahit kulang ang detalye.
At maraming Kristiyano ang bumibigay dito.
Kapag tahimik ang langit. Kapag delayed ang pangako. Kapag hindi malinaw ang susunod.
Pero doon madalas gumagawa ng malalalim na tao ang Diyos.
Sa paghihintay.
Matagal naghintay si Abraham.
Taon. Dekada.
Habang tumatanda si Sarah. Habang parang imposibleng mangyari ang pangako.
Pero sinabi pa rin ng Diyos:
“So shall thy seed be.”
Genesis 15:
וְהֶאֱמִן בַּיהוָה
Vehe’emin BaYHWH
“And he believed in the LORD.”
Ang salitang “believed” ay mula sa Hebrew na:
אָמַן
Aman
Dito rin nanggaling ang salitang “Amen.”
Ibig sabihin:
Buong bigat mong sumandal.
Hindi lang intellectual agreement.
Si Abraham sumandal sa Diyos kahit mukhang imposible ang lahat.
Iyon ang totoong pananampalataya.
Hindi kawalan ng takot.
Kundi pagpili sa Diyos kahit may takot.
At oo, nagkamali rin si Abraham.
Nagsinungaling siya. Nagduda siya. Sinubukan niyang tulungan ang pangako ng Diyos sa pamamagitan ni Hagar.
Hindi tinatago ng Bibliya ang kahinaan ng mga bayani nito.
Dahil ang bida talaga ay hindi si Abraham.
Ang bida ay ang katapatan ng Diyos.
Isa sa pinakamalalim na bahagi ng kuwento niya ay Genesis 15.
Sa covenant noon, parehong dadaan ang dalawang partido sa pagitan ng hinating hayop bilang simbolo:
“Kapag sinira ko ang kasunduang ito, mangyari rin sana ito sa akin.”
Pero sa kuwento ni Abraham, nakatulog siya.
At Diyos lang ang dumaan.
Ibig sabihin?
Alam na ng Diyos na magkakamali si Abraham.
Pero pinili pa rin Siyang maging tapat.
Iyan ang grasya.
May nagbabasa nito ngayon na pakiramdam disqualified ka na dahil sa failures mo.
Pero tandaan mo ito:
Hindi nagulat ang Diyos sa kahinaan mo.
Alam na Niya lahat bago ka pa Niya tawagin.
Hindi excuse ang kasalanan.
Pero patunay ito na ang grasya ay para sa mga sirang tao.
At pagkatapos ng mahabang paghihintay, dumating si Isaac.
Ang anak ng pangako.
Ang himala pagkatapos ng maraming luha.
Pero pagkatapos noon, dumating ang pinakamabigat na pagsubok.
Genesis 22.
“Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest…”
Sa Hebrew:
אֲשֶׁר־אָהַבְתָּ
Asher-Ahavta
“Ang anak na mahal na mahal mo.”
Nakakagulat na ang unang malinaw na paggamit ng salitang “love” sa Bibliya ay konektado sa surrender.
Hindi romance. Hindi comfort.
Kundi pagsuko.
Hiniling ng Diyos kay Abraham na ilagay maging ang pangako sa altar.
Dahil kahit ang mga biyaya ng Diyos puwedeng maging idolo.
May mga taong ginagawang diyos ang relasyon. Ang iba career. Ang iba ministry. Ang iba pangarap.
Pero ipinakita ng Diyos kay Abraham:
Walang dapat mas mahal kaysa sa Diyos mismo.
At habang paakyat sila ng bundok, sinabi ni Abraham:
“God will provide himself a lamb.”
Sa Hebrew:
יְהוָה יִרְאֶה
YHWH Yireh
Jehovah Jireh.
Madalas itong isalin bilang:
“The Lord will provide.”
Pero mas malalim pa roon.
“The Lord will see ahead.”
Nakikita na ng Diyos ang pangangailangan mo bago pa ito dumating.
Nakahanda na ang lalaking tupang ipapalit kay Isaac bago pa sila umakyat ng bundok.
At baka may kailangang makarinig nito ngayon:
Hindi nahuhuli ang provision ng Diyos.
Nakikita na Niya ang bukas mo.
Ang buong kuwento ni Abraham ay tumuturo kay Jesus.
Isang minamahal na anak. Isang ama. Isang bundok. Kahoy na pasan. Isang kapalit na handog.
Mula pa Genesis, bumubulong na ang Ebanghelyo.
At baka kaya malalim tumama ang kuwento ni Abraham dahil nakikita natin ang sarili natin sa kanya.
Takot. Paghihintay. Pagkabigo. Pagdududa. Pagod.
Pero patuloy pa ring lumalakad papunta sa Diyos.
At baka ikaw iyon ngayon.
Pagod ka na. Tahimik ang langit. Pakiramdam mo delayed ang pangako. Pakiramdam mo hindi ka na magagamit ng Diyos.
Pero sumisigaw pa rin ang kuwento ni Abraham:
Tapat pa rin ang Diyos.
Hindi pa tapos ang kuwento mo.
At ang pinakamagandang pangako ng Diyos ay hindi lupa o kayamanan.
Si Jesus.
Siya ang katuparan. Siya ang pag-asa. Siya ang dahilan kung bakit may redemption pa.
Maging totoo ka. Mas malalim ito kaysa simpleng article.
May mga bundok na akala mo katapusan mo, pero doon pala ipapakilala ng Diyos kung sino talaga Siya.
